title: With Due Respect (Vol. 3) -- Ch. 3: Role of the Judicial and Bar Council
keywords: Role of the Judicial and Bar Council
primary_topics: Chapter 3 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 3) -- CJP's September 9, 2007 Inquirer column on the role of the Judicial and Bar Council (JBC) in securing a credible judiciary, opening with why judicial independence matters: an unelected court that upholds a citizen's rights becomes 'a majority of one against the whole government'

His standard for choosing magistrates -- the four 'nis' (independence, integrity, industry, intelligence) and immunity to 'the plague of ships' (kinship, relationship, friendship, fellowship) -- with independence and integrity 'the most vital'

How the old system worked and failed: presidential latitude plus Commission on Appointments (CA) confirmation that subjected appointees to 'intensive questioning' and 'personal demands for favors,' diminishing their integrity and independence -- leading the 1987 Constitution (at Chief Justice Concepcion's suggestion) to create the JBC, limiting the President to a list of at least three nominees with no CA confirmation

The JBC's composition and its weaknesses: a seven-seat body (in practice eight, with two members of Congress) in which the legislature holds two votes, the lingering risk that a President can still 'pack' the courts, and the standing criticisms of opacity, unfilled vacancies and 'unworthy nominees'
sub_topics: Why judicial independence matters: Congress makes laws and the President enforces them, but 'unelected judges decide legal questions by applying relevant laws to a proven set of facts,' so a court upholding a citizen's rights becomes 'a majority of one against the whole government' -- a power citizens obey out of constitutional authority and 'implicit trust in the wisdom and fairness' of the decisions

The marks of a good magistrate: the four 'nis' -- independence, integrity, industry and intelligence -- and immunity to 'the plague of ships' (kinship, relationship, friendship, fellowship), with independence and integrity 'the most vital,' especially in cases against the President; 'a judge who does not possess independence and integrity does not deserve to be in the judiciary, in the same manner that a biased basketball referee has no place in the game'

The old appointment system: the President had 'maximum latitude,' but appointees needed confirmation by the Commission on Appointments, whose members subjected them to 'intensive questioning' and 'personal demands for favors,' demanded the loyalty of district judges, and publicly ridiculed promotions -- diminishing integrity and independence through 'political power plays'

The JBC's creation: the 1987 Constitution, at former Chief Justice Roberto Concepcion's suggestion, created the JBC with 'the principal function of recommending appointees to the Judiciary,' limiting the President to a list of 'at least three nominees for every vacancy' and abolishing CA confirmation -- freeing magistrates from 'undue congressional inquisitions'

Composition: the JBC's seven seats -- the Chief Justice (chair), the secretary of justice, and a representative of Congress (the three 'ex-officio members'), plus representatives of the Integrated Bar, the legal academe, the retired Supreme Court justices, and the private sector (the four 'regular members')

The two-Congress wrinkle: in practice a senator and a congressman both sit, making eight members (each with one vote), so approval needs five of eight (not four of seven) and the legislature holds two votes to the other branches' one each; a proposal during CJP's term to cut the congressional vote to one was abandoned because resolving it required an 'adversarial proceeding'; the four regular members are presidential appointees confirmed by the CA for renewable four-year terms

The residual 'packing' risk and the criticisms: appointees are now shielded from direct congressional influence, but JBC members are not, and 'nothing except the highest form of statesmanship' stops a politically minded President from steering the Council's choices -- so a President 'could still pack the courts'; the JBC has also been faulted for opacity and a 'lackluster' process, for failing to fill vacancies (aggravating delays), and for listing 'unworthy nominees' who get appointed and 'taint the whole judiciary'

stances.claim: Because an independent court can rule for a citizen as 'a majority of one against the whole government,' magistrates must be chosen prudently for the four 'nis' (independence, integrity, industry, intelligence) and be immune to 'the plague of ships' -- with independence and integrity the most vital.
stances.rhetorical_move: first-principles setup: grounding the selection standard in the awesome, anti-majoritarian power of judging

stances.claim: The JBC was a genuine improvement on the old Commission-on-Appointments system, which diminished judges' independence through 'intensive questioning' and 'personal demands for favors' -- but it remains imperfect, since a President 'could still pack the courts' by steering a Council whose members (unlike judges) are not shielded from political pressure.
stances.rhetorical_move: reform-with-caveat: crediting the Concepcion innovation while exposing its residual loophole

stances.claim: The JBC's structure and conduct invite legitimate criticism -- opacity, a 'lackluster' nomination process, unfilled vacancies that aggravate delay, and 'unworthy nominees' who taint the judiciary -- setting up the case for reform.
stances.rhetorical_move: problem-cataloguing: listing the JBC's faults to prepare the follow-up reform column

notable_anecdotes: 'A majority of one': CJP captures the power of judicial independence in the image of a court that, upholding one citizen's rights, stands 'a majority of one against the whole government.'
The biased referee: he reprises his favorite analogy -- a judge lacking independence and integrity 'has no place' on the bench, just as 'a biased basketball referee has no place in the game.'
The Concepcion innovation: he credits former Chief Justice Roberto Concepcion with suggesting the JBC to rescue appointees from the Commission on Appointments' 'personal demands for favors.'

Two votes for Congress: he flags the practical quirk that, with both a senator and a congressman sitting, the legislature holds two of the JBC's eight votes -- and that a move to cut it to one was dropped during his term.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 3 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 3), CJP's September 9, 2007 Inquirer column, explains the role of the Judicial and Bar Council (JBC) in securing a credible judiciary. He begins with why independence matters: where Congress makes laws and the President enforces them, 'unelected judges' decide legal questions by applying law to facts, so a court that upholds a citizen's rights becomes 'a majority of one against the whole government' -- a power obeyed because of constitutional authority and 'implicit trust' in the courts' fairness. Magistrates must therefore be chosen for the four 'nis' (independence, integrity, industry, intelligence) and be immune to 'the plague of ships' (kinship, relationship, friendship, fellowship), with independence and integrity most vital -- 'a judge who does not possess independence and integrity... has no place' on the bench, 'in the same manner that a biased basketball referee has no place in the game.' Under the old system, he recalls, the President had wide latitude but appointees faced Commission on Appointments confirmation that subjected them to 'intensive questioning' and 'personal demands for favors,' diminishing their independence -- so the 1987 Constitution, at Chief Justice Concepcion's suggestion, created the JBC to recommend appointees, limiting the President to a list of at least three per vacancy and abolishing CA confirmation. He details the JBC's seven seats (three ex-officio, four regular) and the practical wrinkle that two members of Congress sit, giving the legislature two of eight votes and raising the approval threshold to five. Yet the reform is incomplete: appointees are shielded from Congress, but JBC members are not, and 'nothing except the highest form of statesmanship' stops a President from steering the Council -- so a President 'could still pack the courts.' He closes by listing the JBC's standing criticisms -- opacity and a 'lackluster' process, unfilled vacancies that aggravate delay, and 'unworthy nominees' who get appointed and 'taint the whole judiciary' -- setting up his follow-up column on reforming it.
